title: Namo brahmaṇe: a prayer not to forget
theme: A prayer to retain what has been heard: may it be held and not slip away.

words.context: Anonymous and Sāyaṇa: «ब्रह्मणे जगत्कारणाय» — to Brahman, the cause of the world
Sāyaṇa: «ग्रन्थतदर्थयोर्धारणमस्तु» — retention of the text and its meaning
Sāyaṇa: «निराकरणं विस्मरणं यथा न भवति तथा» — so that there is no forgetting

words.role: subject in sense of mā cyoḍhvam

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «हे देवा मा च्योढ्वं मा विनाशयत» — gods, do not let it be lost
Anonymous and Sāyaṇa: «अमुष्येत्थं प्रार्थयमानस्य मम» — of me, the one praying thus; Bhāskara: «अद इति परं ब्रह्माह» — that, the supreme Brahman

sandhi.rule: A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant.

sandhi_exceptions.note: me · astu: the e of me is not joined to the following a (classical me ’stu); every witness prints them apart, as Vedic texts often do.
amuṣya · om: the a is not joined to om (classical amuṣyom); Bhāskara notes the hiatus as natural here («ईषाअक्षादित्वात् प्रकृतिभावः»).

morphology.note: Second person plural middle of √cyu without augment, used with mā as a prohibition. Sāyaṇa supplies the gods as the persons addressed; Bhāskara the senses («हे तत्परिपन्थीनि! इन्द्रियाणि!»).
An agent noun in -tṛ used with bhūyāsam: ‘may I be a holder’, i.e. may I retain.

translation.literal: Homage to Brahman. Let there be retention in me; may I be a holder without forgetting. What is heard in the ears — do not let it slip — of me, of that one. Om.
translation.readable: Homage to Brahman. May I hold what I have learned, and keep it without forgetting; let what my ears have heard not slip away from me. Om.

syntax: A salutation (namo brahmaṇe), a wish with astu, a wish with the precative bhūyāsam, and a prohibition with mā and the injunctive cyoḍhvam, whose subject or addressee is left to be supplied; mama amuṣya names the speaker.

ambiguities.note: The plural cyoḍhvam has no stated subject. Sāyaṇa addresses the gods («हे देवा»), the anonymous commentator a god, Bhāskara the senses that draw the mind away.

‘Of that one’: the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read it as the speaker (‘of me, the one praying thus’, a place for one’s own name); Bhāskara reads it as the supreme Brahman, with whom the speaker is one («तदात्मनो ब्रह्मीभूतस्य मम»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose prayer, one printed line of 36 syllables; no metre is claimed.

beginner: A short prayer that what one has learned should stay. It begins with homage to Brahman, then asks: may I hold what I have learned, may I keep it without forgetting, and may what my ears have heard not slip away. In ancient India knowledge was carried by memory, heard from a teacher and repeated until it was fixed, so forgetting meant losing it. The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa say this is a prayer, recited quietly, for keeping the Vedas one has received. Bhāskara reads it more inwardly: the holding is a steady focus on Brahman, and it is the senses that are told not to wander. The record reports these readings and claims nothing about what reciting it does.
analogy: Like asking a cupped hand not to open before the water reaches the mouth.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It pays homage to Brahman, asks that there be retention in the speaker and that the speaker hold without forgetting, and asks that what the ears have heard should not slip away; it closes with om.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: a japa for not forgetting the Vedas one has received — «अथ लब्धानां वेदानामविस्मरणाय जप्यं मन्त्रमाह». Brahman is greeted as the cause of the world, and by its grace there should be retention of both the text and its meaning: «तत्प्रसादान्मदीये चित्ते ग्रन्थतदर्थयोर्धारणमस्तु».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For Bhāskara the holding is one-pointedness, becoming one with Brahman: «तद्भावापत्तिस् तदर्थं धारणम् ऐकाग्र्यं मे अस्तु». The plural ‘do not slip’ is addressed to the senses, which have enjoyed their objects until now and must not now fall away from Brahman: «यूयं मा च्योढ्वं मा ब्रह्मणश्च्युतानि भूत».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Only one difference is listed for this anuvāka, a slip in one witness. The hiatus in मे अस्त्व् and अमुष्य ओम् is in every witness.

schools.disagreement: The commentaries available are ritual and Vedic; Bhāskara’s reading points toward union with Brahman, but none of the three takes a position on which the Vedānta schools named here divide. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here).

contemporary.text: The prayer treats forgetting as the real danger to learning, and asks not for more knowledge but for keeping what has been received. Revisiting what one has already learned before seeking more is still sound advice. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What is one thing you learned long ago that you are glad you never forgot?
reflect.deeper: Is the “holding” here memory (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa) or concentration (Bhāskara)? Can the two be separated?
reflect.practice: Recall something you learned last week, without looking it up, and write it down.

flags.note: amuṣya (‘of that one’) is the speaker for the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman for Bhāskara.
